sentences.text: The herd on the Cairngorms is free-ranging over about four hundred hectares of the high plateau and it comes down to the enclosure at Glenmore when it wants to, which is mostly in the winter, and there is nothing at all mysterious about that.
There is grazing up there in summer and there is not much in December.

Reindeer are extremely good at digging for lichen through snow and extremely bad at coping with the wet warm winters that part of Scotland has been getting, and when the tops go hard they come down and the herders put food out and everybody is happy.
That is what the visitors are told and it is true.
Morag has said it perhaps two thousand times.

It is on a laminated card and it is in the talk and it is what she tells the families who come up the hill in waterproofs in July to see reindeer in a Scottish summer and are usually surprised by how much they smell.
What Morag was told, by her mother, who has worked with that herd since 2004, is the other thing.
The herd comes down when it likes.
Some of them come down in October and some hang about until January and there is no order to it that anybody has ever been able to chart.
Except the bull.

There is one bull — his name in the herd book is a number and the herders call him something else that Morag is not going to write down, because that name is theirs and she does not think it belongs in a story — and he comes down alone, ahead of everything, in a straight line off the Cairn Lochan side.
And it snows within about thirty hours.
Morag grew up with this the way other children grow up with a family saying.

Her mother would come in and take her boots off and say *he's down*, and Morag's father would look at the window, and there would be snow on the tops by the following afternoon, and nobody ever remarked on it because remarking on it would have been like remarking that the kettle had boiled.
Not sometimes.
Every year that anybody in that family has kept track of, and Morag's mother has kept track since 2004 in a notebook that also has feed orders and a recipe for flapjack in it.
Twenty-one years.
Twenty-one first snows on the plateau, twenty-one bulls walking down off Cairn Lochan somewhere between one and thirty hours before, and eighteen of them accurate to within a day.
It is not always the same animal.

That is the part visitors get stuck on and that Morag's mother is brisk about: a bull is good for perhaps eleven or twelve years and there have been four of them in twenty-one, and each one has done it, and nobody taught them, and there is no lineage — the current one is not the son of the last.
What there is, as far as anybody in that family can see, is a plateau, and a set of conditions on it, and whichever animal happens to be the one that notices first.
